issues.legal_issue: The presumption that stored foodgrains are held for sale does not apply to a person who proves that they are an agriculturist.
material_facts: Foodgrains exceeding the permitted quantities were found stored in a godown, and the accused did not hold a dealer’s licence.
The accused produced lease deeds, receipts for lease payments, and oral testimony that he and his brother cultivated 80–90 bighas of land on which the foodgrains were grown.
The Court accepted the combined evidence as showing that the accused was carrying on agricultural operations.
issues.conclusion: Because the accused proved that he was an agriculturist, the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn against him. Without that presumption, the prosecution’s case was unproved, so the conviction and forfeiture order were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrains Dealer’s Licensing Order, 1966 excludes bona fide consumers and agriculturists from the presumption that storage of foodgrains is for sale; the provision concerns storage for sale as part of dealing in foodgrains. The prosecution was under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act. The Court referred to Manipur Administration v. M. Nila Chandra Singh, which described business as ordinarily involving a course of conduct and continuity of transactions, but said it need not decide that question in this case and noted that even one transaction may be in the course of business depending on the circumstances.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_unlicensed_food: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution alleging dealing in foodgrains without the required authorization.
predicates.foodgrains_stored_above_permitted_quanti: The accused stored foodgrains in quantities exceeding the applicable permitted limit.
predicates.agriculturist_status_proved_by_supportin: The accused presented evidence supporting that the stored foodgrains came from agricultural operations carried on by the accused.
predicates.conviction_cannot_stand_on_storage_alone: A conviction cannot stand when storage alone supplies the basis for the prosecution against a person proved to be an agriculturist.

issues.definition: When a criminal prosecution rests on above-limit storage and the accused proves through supporting evidence that the foodgrains came from the accused’s agricultural operations, storage alone does not sustain the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered lease deed may be considered in a criminal case to establish a collateral fact about possession of land for cultivation.
material_facts: The accused relied on unregistered lease deeds relating to land he said he cultivated.
The trial court rejected the deeds as inadmissible, while the appellate court questioned their reliability because they could have been created at any time.
The Supreme Court held that the deeds could serve the collateral purpose of showing that the land described by the witnesses was held for cultivation.
issues.conclusion: The lease deeds were not to be excluded merely because they were unregistered; they could be considered for the collateral purpose of showing that the land was held for cultivation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act was invoked against the deeds, but the Court held that in a criminal case their genuineness and evidentiary value had to be assessed and that they could be used for a collateral purpose, rather than being rejected solely for want of registration. No earlier case was relied on for this point.

predicates.lease_documents_are_unregistered: The party relying on the lease documents has not registered them.
predicates.lease_documents_offered_to_show_cultivat: The party offers the lease documents to support that land was held for cultivation, rather than to prove a matter requiring registration.
predicates.unregistered_lease_documents_may_support: Unregistered lease documents may be considered as evidence of collateral facts.

issues.definition: In a criminal case concerning land possession, unregistered lease documents offered to show cultivation-related possession may support collateral facts.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s status as a next-door neighbour does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: Witnesses gave oral evidence that the accused and his brother cultivated the land from which the stored foodgrains came.
The trial and appellate courts rejected the oral evidence as unreliable because the witnesses were next-door neighbours and were considered interested in the accused.
The Supreme Court found no adequate reason for rejection and stated that such testimony could be rejected only if something was intrinsically wrong with it.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony could not properly be rejected merely because they were next-door neighbours; there had to be something intrinsically wrong with the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the evidentiary principle that a witness’s proximity to a party does not alone make the witness’s testimony unreliable; the testimony may be rejected on that basis only where it is intrinsically flawed. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.
